courses.title: CARSI Carpet Cleaning Workshop (2-Day)
courses.description: A two-day, hands-on carpet and upholstery cleaning workshop run by CARSI on the Sydney roadshow, 30 to 31 July 2026. Day 1 covers safety and standards, fibre science, cleaning chemistry, the five cleaning principles and spot and stain removal. Day 2 covers upholstery fabric and construction, upholstery methods, hard-floor inspection and cleaning, machinery maintenance, the business of cleaning and a seven-role expert case review. Four follow-on modules cover advanced stain removal, strip and seal, add-on services and marketing. Every module is taught at three levels, Newby, Intermediate and Pro, with a quiz for each. Attending both days earns a CARSI certificate of attendance. This workshop carries no IICRC CECs. Delivered on the CARSI roadshow with partner venue Carpet Cleaners Warehouse (CCW).

lessons.title: How the two days run
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Describe what you will do on Day 1 and Day 2 and why the course is hands-on.
  • Place yourself at the Newby, Intermediate or Pro level and say what you want from each module.
  • Explain what the certificate of attendance needs.

This is a workshop, not a lecture. By the end of Day 2 you will have done every core technique at least once with a trainer watching. The course is CARSI original material, taught by Phill McGurk, and the take-home manual is a CARSI document. It refers to published standards but does not copy them.

The two days

DayModuleTime allowed
Day 1Module 1: Welcome to the Workshop: Safety and Standards60 minutes
Day 1Module 2: Fibre Science75 minutes
Day 1Module 3: Chemistry of Cleaning90 minutes
Day 1Module 4: The Five Cleaning Principles (hands-on)105 minutes
Day 1Module 5: Spot and Stain Removal105 minutes
Day 2Module 6: Upholstery Theory: Fibre and Fabric Construction90 minutes
Day 2Module 7: Upholstery Hands-On135 minutes
Day 2Module 8: Hard Floors75 minutes
Day 2Module 9: Machinery and Preventive Maintenance90 minutes
Day 2Module 10: The Business of Cleaning60 minutes
Day 2Module 11: Expert Board Case Review45 minutes

Modules 12 to 15 in this course go further on stains, then strip and seal, then add-on services and marketing. They are written for you to read after the workshop days.

Three levels in every module

  • Newby: under 12 months in the industry. You are learning the vocabulary, the safe defaults and the five cleaning principles.
  • Intermediate: one to five years on the tools, with formal training behind you. You are ready for chemistry choices and for working out why a job went wrong.
  • Pro: five years or more. You are working on edge cases, pricing, inspection-grade judgement and training other people.

Every module ends with a take-away for each level. Read all three and ask where you actually are, not where you would like to be. Being honest about it is the fastest way to improve.

How the figures in this course are labelled

Where a number comes from a published source, the lesson says so. Where it is CARSI professional judgement, such as a rule of thumb from the trainer, the lesson says that instead. Nothing here is invented to fill a gap.

The certificate

Attending both days earns a CARSI certificate of attendance. You need to be checked in on Day 1 and again on Day 2. The workshop does not carry IICRC CECs.

lessons.title: Standards and your scope of work
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Name the IICRC standard that covers each kind of work in the table.
  • Say which jobs a carpet technician takes on and which ones to document and refer.
  • Explain the water category stop rule.

The IICRC publishes a family of ANSI consensus standards that mark out professional scope for carpet and textile floor coverings and for restoration work. Knowing which one governs a job is the first step to working inside your scope, and to knowing when to call a specialist.

StandardCoversYour role as a carpet technician
ANSI/IICRC S100Cleaning of textile floor coveringsPrimary reference for carpet cleaning
ANSI/IICRC S300Upholstery cleaningPrimary reference for fabric and soft furniture
ANSI/IICRC S220Inspection of hard-surface floorsInspection scope for tile, stone, resilient floors and timber
ANSI/IICRC S500Water damage restorationRecognise Category 1, Category 2 and Category 3 water and know when to stop
ANSI/IICRC S520Mould remediationRecognise visible mould. It is outside this workshop's scope
ANSI/IICRC S540Trauma and crime-scene cleaningNot within a carpet technician's scope without the right credentials
ANSI/IICRC S700Fire and smoke restorationSoot on carpet: refer to a restorer
ANSI/IICRC S800Inspection of textile floor coveringsThe inspector's scope. You support it with documentation

This table is a CARSI summary of scope. For the definitive wording, buy and read the standards from the IICRC.

Why cite a standard at all

A technician who can say "I followed the published standard for this job and wrote down what I did" is in a far stronger position than one who says "that is how I have always done it". That is professional judgement, not a legal rule, but it holds up on every complaint you will ever deal with.

Know when to stop

You can clean after a Category 1 (clean water) intrusion within your scope. Category 2 (grey water with significant contamination) and Category 3 (grossly contaminated water, for example sewage) need restorers trained to the water damage standard. If you are in doubt, stop, then photograph it, write it up and refer it. Working outside your scope is a liability, not a favour to the customer.

lessons.title: Safety you do not negotiate
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • List the personal protective equipment for chemical work and for truck-mount work.
  • State what you must carry for every chemical you use.
  • Explain the electrical and slip controls on a wet job.

Every cleaner handles chemicals. The alkaline pre-spray that lifts grease from a commercial carpet can blister skin on contact and hurt your lungs if you breathe the mist for an hour. Safety is the first skill of the trade.

Personal protective equipment

  • Nitrile gloves for chemical handling, as a minimum. Replace them when they tear.
  • Safety glasses when you spray overhead or use a high-pressure wand.
  • A P2 respirator when you atomise stronger alkalines or use dry compounds.
  • Closed-toe, non-slip footwear on every job.
  • Hearing protection around a running truck-mount. The manual puts typical levels at 85 dBA and above.

Hazardous chemicals

  • Keep a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) in the vehicle for every chemical you use. In most Australian jurisdictions the WHS regulations require one on site for each hazardous chemical in use.
  • Label every decanted container with the product, the hazard and the date.
  • Write an exposure control plan that lists the likely exposures and the protective equipment for each task.
  • Know the first aid section of the SDS by heart. Phone the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 if someone is exposed.

Electrical, water, slips and heat

  • Plug portable extractors into a circuit protected by an RCD (safety switch). Press the test button at the start of every job.
  • Portable electrical equipment should be tested and tagged to AS/NZS 3760 on its schedule.
  • Run cables along walls and put up signs and door wedges to manage trips.
  • Put out "Wet Floor" signs until the floor meets its drying target (see Module 4).
  • Watch for heat stress in hot, strenuous work and rotate people through the hands-on stations.

New Zealand

In New Zealand the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 and WorkSafe New Zealand apply in place of the Australian WHS laws and regulators. Where this course names an Australian regulator or rule, check the New Zealand position on worksafe.govt.nz, and on epa.govt.nz for hazardous substances, before you rely on it. The AS/NZS standards, 230 V and 50 Hz supply and metric units are the same on both sides of the Tasman.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Know the standard families and which one covers which job. Know which protective equipment goes on before which chemistry.
  • Intermediate: Know which standard governs the scope of work. Build an exposure control plan for your own business.
  • Pro: Understand how a published recommendation differs from a requirement, and how standards are revised over time.

lessons.title: The three fibre families
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Sort the common carpet and upholstery fibres into synthetic, protein or cellulosic families.
  • Say why fibre identification comes before any other decision.

Fibre identification is the highest-value skill in carpet cleaning. Every later choice, from chemistry to temperature to agitation to drying, is limited by the fibre in front of you. Get it wrong and you will either under-clean the job or damage the fibre beyond repair.

Synthetic (petroleum-based, mostly)

  • Nylon 6 and nylon 6,6: the dominant residential and commercial fibre. Resilient, takes dye well and is sensitive to pH.
  • Polyester (PET): low cost, hydrophobic, strong stain resistance and poor resilience.
  • Triexta: corn-derived, with built-in stain resistance.
  • Olefin (polypropylene): solution-dyed, so the colour runs right through. Poor resilience and a low heat tolerance.
  • Acrylic: imitates wool and is less common in modern carpet.

Protein (animal)

  • Wool: a warm hand, self-extinguishing, prefers acidic chemistry and must never be over-wetted.
  • Silk: very sensitive to moisture and to alkaline chemistry. Inspect and refer antique pieces.

Cellulosic (plant)

Cotton, linen, rayon, acetate, jute, sisal, coir. Rayon can lose up to 70 per cent of its strength when wet, so keep moisture and agitation low.

lessons.title: Identifying a fibre: hand, then burn, then float
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Run the field sequence of hand-feel, burn test and float test on a tuft.
  • Read the result against the burn table and the field card.

In the field the reliable order is hand-feel first, then a burn test to confirm. A burn test on a single tuft taken from an inconspicuous spot is decisive. Pluck the tuft over a non-flammable surface, keep chemicals well away, and have water to hand. That precaution is CARSI practice, not a figure from a standard.

FibreBurn behaviourHand and odour
WoolBurns slowly, self-extinguishes, leaves crushable black ashWarm and springy, burnt-hair smell
SilkBurns slowly, similar to wool, faint smellSmooth, cool, slight lustre
Cotton or linenBurns freely with an afterglow, fluffy grey ashMatte, soaks up water at once
RayonBurns like cotton, very fastSoft, weakens badly when wet
NylonMelts and burns, leaves a hard grey or tan bead, celery-like smellResilient, springs back
PolyesterMelts and burns, leaves a hard black bead, sweet smellSmooth, low resilience
OlefinMelts then burns, sooty smoke, waxy smellWaxy hand, even solution-dyed colour

The field card, step by step

  1. Hand-feel. A warm, springy, slightly oily feel suggests wool. A smooth, cool, lustrous feel suggests silk or rayon. Waxy with even colour suggests olefin. Springing back suggests nylon.
  2. Burn one tuft. Self-extinguishing with a burnt-hair smell points to wool or silk. A hard grey bead with a celery smell is nylon. A hard black bead with a sweet smell is polyester. Sooty smoke with a waxy smell is olefin. Paper-like fluffy ash is cotton or another cellulosic.
  3. Float a fibre in cool water. If it floats, it is olefin. Most other fibres sink.

On day one you will rotate through the burn and float stations, plus solubility and hand-feel so you can feel the differences, not just read about them.

lessons.title: The fibre fence and the weakest-member rule
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Read the pH limit, the temperature limit and the agitation tolerance for each fibre from the table.
  • Apply the weakest-member rule to a blended fibre.

Every fibre has a chemistry fence. Cross it and you damage the fibre. The table below is CARSI's rule-of-thumb starting point. Always check the manufacturer's care instructions when you can get them.

FibrepH rangeMaximum water temperatureAgitation tolerance
Nylon5.5 to 10 (never above 10)60 to 80 °CMedium to high
Polyester5.5 to 1060 to 80 °CMedium
Triexta5.5 to 1060 to 80 °CMedium to high
Olefin5.5 to 1060 °C maximum (low melt point)Medium
Wool4.5 to 8 (acidic preferred)40 °C maximumLow
Silk4.5 to 7.5Ambient to 35 °CVery low
RayonNeutral, 6 to 8Ambient to 35 °CVery low (loses strength when wet)
Cotton6 to 9Ambient to 50 °CLow to medium

The weakest-member rule

On a blend, the more delicate fibre decides the chemistry. Treat an 80 per cent wool, 20 per cent nylon blend as wool. A 50/50 silk and cotton drapery is silk for pH purposes.

Common mistake

Cleaning an unlabelled rug with a nylon-strength pre-spray and hot water because the pile "looks like nylon". If you have not burn-tested it, assume the more delicate fibre until you have proved otherwise.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Name five fibres by sight and burn test. Know that wool and nylon need different chemistry.
  • Intermediate: Map fibre to its pH range, temperature limit and agitation tolerance on any carpet in the field. Spot-test rayon before you wet it.
  • Pro: Call the weakest-member rule on blends and explain why cationic surfactants damage the dye blockers on nylon.

lessons.title: Module 2 Knowledge Check: Fibre Science
pH in practice and the two rules you do not break
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Place a product in the right pH zone and say what it is for.
  • State the nylon pH ceiling and the wool finish rule.
  • Check a final rinse with a pH strip the right way.

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. CARSI uses practical zones, written as our own working guide.

ZonepH rangePractical meaning
Strong acid0 to 3Rust removers and acidic dye-set products. Use with care
Mild acid4 to 6Wool finish rinses and general acidic neutralisers
Neutral6 to 8Test default, safe on most fibres
Mild alkaline8 to 10General pre-spray zone for synthetic fibres
Strong alkalineAbove 10Degreasers. Never go above 10 on nylon

Two rules you do not break

  • Nylon pH ceiling: 10. Go over it and you strip the acid-dye sites, which shows up as colour loss.
  • Wool finish: acidic, pH 4.5 to 6.5. Skip it and you yellow the wool and roughen the hand.

Read the substrate, not the bottle

A pH strip dipped in the pre-spray bottle tells you about the bottle. A damp strip pressed to the cleaned carpet tells you what the fibre is actually holding. The two numbers can be 1.0 to 2.0 units apart, because fibres such as wool and cotton buffer acid and alkaline differently. Your callback risk sits in the second number.

Final rinse target

Aim for a final substrate pH of 6.5 to 8.0. That helps prevent re-soiling, browning or yellowing. Press a fresh strip to a damp spot after extraction. It takes 15 seconds. If the reading is outside the range, re-rinse with a matched pH-correcting product.

lessons.title: Surfactants, soil classes and CHAT
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Name the four surfactant families and one thing each is used for.
  • Sort soil into its three classes and name the first action for each.
  • Trade one CHAT dial against another for a given job.

Surfactant families

A surfactant is the bridge between water and soil. The one you choose affects cleaning power, residue, re-soiling and how well it sits with the fibre's dye system.

  • Anionic: the workhorse. Strong detergency and good foam. It can leave a sticky residue if rinsed badly.
  • Cationic: disinfecting and antistatic. It damages the acid-dye blockers on nylon, so avoid it on nylon carpet.
  • Non-ionic: low foaming and good with solvents. Common in pre-sprays.
  • Amphoteric: changes charge with pH. Gentle, and used in wool-safe formulas.

Soil classes

  • Water-soluble (sugar, urine salts, beverages): any aqueous cleaning removes it.
  • Solvent-soluble (oils, grease, tar, ink): needs emulsifying or a solvent.
  • Insoluble (sand, grit, fibre): removed mechanically by vacuuming and pile-lifting.

Every dirty carpet is a mix of all three. Principle 1 (dry soil removal) takes most of the insoluble soil. Principle 2 (suspension) lifts the water-soluble and solvent-soluble soil with chemistry.

CHAT: four dials you control

Chemistry, Heat, Agitation and Time. You can trade one for another inside the fibre fence. Lower the pH and you can add heat or time. Lower the temperature and you can add agitation. Shorten the dwell and you can raise the chemistry strength. The skill is knowing which dial to turn on which fibre.

  1. A cold job in winter: add dwell time and go slightly higher in pH, within the fence, to make up for the lost heat.
  2. A delicate wool rug: keep pH down and heat down, then make up with a longer dwell and gentler agitation.
  3. Heavy commercial grease on nylon: pH 10 at most, plus heat, soft agitation and an 8 to 10 minute dwell.

lessons.title: Wool and the pH 7 myth
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Explain what the WoolSafe mark does and does not mean.
  • Say why alkalinity matters more than pH alone on wool, together with heat and dwell.

The most common belief in carpet cleaning is that pH 7 means wool-safe. It does not.

WoolSafe is a certification mark run by an independent organisation in Otley, in the United Kingdom. A product earns it only by passing the organisation's test methods and holding a current licence to show the mark. A product sold as "wool-safe" or "wool-compatible" without the mark is making an uncertified claim. It may still suit wool. It has not been through the test panel.

The real criterion is alkalinity

The published criterion is a limit on alkalinity, which is how much acid the solution resists. It is not a limit on pH. The working figures are these:

  • An alkaline pre-spray passes if no more than 5 mL of 0.1 N hydrochloric acid brings 100 mL of working solution down to pH 7, and no more than 14 mL brings it down to pH 5.5.
  • An acid-side rinse must stay at pH 2.5 or higher.

So a certified pre-spray can read as high as about pH 9.5 to 10 at the meter, if its buffering is low enough. Wool damage comes from alkalinity combined with heat and dwell time, not from pH alone.

A practical rule for wool

For routine residential wool, a low-alkalinity pre-spray at pH 9.5 with warm water (not hot) and a prompt acidic rinse is gentler than a pH 8 product with high residual alkalinity left on for 30 minutes. For insurance-grade, antique, museum or specified wool jobs, use a product that is currently on the WoolSafe Approved register at woolsafe.org, and keep a copy of the register entry in the job file.

lessons.title: Product starting points and chemistry safety
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Use the product table as a starting point, not a recipe.
  • State the non-negotiable chemistry safety rules.

The CARSI and CCW Product Guide lists the products stocked by the roadshow partner, with dilutions taken from the supplier pages and safety data sheets. The guide states that it was checked against ccwonline.com.au in April 2026. The label and the SDS always beat any table. Ask the supplier where a figure is not published.

Product (Razorback)pHPublished starting dilutionNotes from the guide
PowerShot UHT pre-spray10.2 to 10.832:1 standard, 8:1 inline, 16:1 upholsteryHigh-alkaline traffic-lane product for commercial nylon. Hot water. Not for wool. Always rinse
BioShot UHT enzyme pre-spray9.5 to 10.550 to 100 g per 10 L pump; 25 g per litre for upholsterySold as wool-compatible but not on the WoolSafe register
SnapShot Extra LMC8.032:1 standard, 8:1 for upholstery and spottingTriple use as an encapsulation product, a bonnet product and a pre-spray. Low residue and low alkalinity
e-Rinse EFR acid rinse2.0 to 2.550 mL per 10 L portable; 500 mL per 10 L for browningBelow the WoolSafe threshold for rinses, so dilute generously and keep contact short on wool. Never on calcareous stone
CitraBoost booster and spotterSee the SDS75 to 150 mL per 10 L as a pre-spray booster; neat on a test area as a spotterSolvent-based. Ventilate well

None of the stocked products in the guide carries the WoolSafe mark. For high-stakes wool work, source a certified product and keep the register entry.

Chemistry safety rules

  1. Never mix acid and chlorine. The gas is lethal.
  2. Never store oxidisers near reducers.
  3. Label every diluted bottle with the date, the product and the dilution.
  4. Decant away from the carpet surface.
  5. Wear gloves and glasses, and a P2 respirator, for every acid-rinse job.
  6. Ventilate when you use solvent boosters.
  7. If the SDS calls for specific protective equipment, use it with no exceptions.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Read a product label. Never mix acids with chlorine. Always rinse.
  • Intermediate: Choose which CHAT dial to turn for a given soil class on a given fibre.
  • Pro: Build a paired pre-spray and rinse that lands the final substrate pH at 6.5 to 8.0, and explain why cationic products hurt nylon blockers.

lessons.title: The five principles in order
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Recite the five principles in order.
  • Explain why Principle 1 is called the multiplier.

The five principles are the spine of carpet cleaning. They apply to every method and every fibre, and the order is fixed. If you skip a step you pay for it later in the job.

  1. Dry particulate soil removal: vacuuming with airflow and agitation.
  2. Soil suspension: chemistry, heat, agitation, time (CHAT).
  3. Extraction of the suspended soil.
  4. Pile setting or grooming: realign the fibres for even drying and finish.
  5. Drying: remove residual moisture to below the fibre's safe threshold.

Skip Principle 1 and you grind grit into the yarn during Principle 2. Skip Principle 5 and you invite browning and wicking, plus microbial growth. The emphasis shifts with the job. On a lightly soiled house, Principle 1 is most of the work. On a heavily soiled commercial carpet, Principles 2 and 3 earn their keep.

Principle 1 in detail

These are CARSI teaching figures, and Station A is where you test them yourself. A good upright with a beater bar takes about 50 to 65 per cent of the dry particulate soil from residential carpet in one pass. A second pass in the cross direction typically takes a further 10 to 20 per cent. Pile lifters help on heavily soiled or crushed commercial carpet. To check, run a clean white cloth along one row of pile after vacuuming. The mark on the cloth is your baseline.

That second pass costs roughly three extra minutes on a 40 square metre house. It needs no new equipment, no new chemistry and no price rise. It is the cheapest upgrade in the trade.

lessons.title: Suspension and extraction
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Say how long a pre-spray should dwell.
  • Name the four extraction methods.
  • Describe the dry-stroke wand technique.

Principle 2: soil suspension

Chemistry separates soil from the fibre. The CHAT dials decide how hard it needs to work. Most pre-sprays need 5 to 10 minutes on the fibre before you rinse to reach full effect.

Principle 3: extraction

There are four main methods: hot water extraction, encapsulation, bonnet or absorbent pad, and dry compound. Hot water extraction is still the leading restorative method, and it is what the hands-on session builds muscle memory for.

  • Dry stroke: on every wand stroke the trigger pull is shorter than the vacuum pull. The typical ratio is 1:2, so half the stroke is dry vacuum only.
  • Wand angle: too steep leaves water behind and too flat loses suction. You learn the feel on the day.
  • Overlap: overlap your strokes by about 25 per cent to avoid stripes.

Plan wand speed and airmover placement before you spray chemistry, not after. Every extra minute of dwell is drying time you owe back.

lessons.title: Grooming and drying
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Explain why you groom the pile after extraction.
  • Set drying targets and an airmover count for a job.

Principle 4: pile setting

After extraction the pile is flat and wet, and it lies unevenly. A pile-setting brush or carpet rake puts the pile direction back, speeds up drying and gives the finished carpet an even look. Leave it out and the carpet dries with wand tracks showing.

Principle 5: drying

Moisture left too long causes browning from cellulosic wicking, wicking stains, microbial growth and complaints. CARSI drying targets:

  • Commercial: back in service in 8 hours or less.
  • Residential: safe to walk on within 2 hours and fully dry within 12 hours.
  • Speed it up with airmovers, one for every 14 to 23 square metres, plus dehumidification in humid weather and the building's air conditioning where it is available.

Common mistake: unpacking chemistry first and thinking about airmovers at the end. By then the carpet is already wet and the clock is running.

lessons.title: The pre-inspection form and the four stations
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Complete the top half of the pre-inspection form before any chemistry touches the fibre.
  • Describe what you do at each of the four stations.

Before you spray anything on a hands-on station you complete the top half of the pre-inspection form. It becomes your permanent job template.

SectionWhat you record
Customer and siteName, address, date, contact details and access notes
Fibre identificationVisible fibre, burn-test result, float result, hand-feel and face-weight estimate
ConstructionTufted or woven, pile type, whether the backing is visible
Pre-existing conditionsWear patterns, stains (with a photo), existing damage and odours
Room environmentRelative humidity, temperature, HVAC status and the ventilation plan
Planned methodHot water extraction, low moisture or dry compound; tool; chemistry and pH; target dwell
Drying planAirmover count and placement, whether a dehumidifier is needed, expected dry time
Customer communicationMoisture addendum signed? Re-entry time given?
Post-clean verificationFinal substrate pH, moisture meter reading and a photo

The four stations (25 minutes each)

  • Station A, dry soil removal: compare an upright with a pile lifter and the third machine your trainer sets out. Weigh the dry soil you remove and check the beater-bar contact.
  • Station B, low-moisture methods: encapsulation, rotary bonnet and dry compound.
  • Station C, hot water extraction: truck-mount against portable. Take water-lift and pressure readings and practise the dry-stroke technique.
  • Station D, drying: airmover placement, dehumidifier sizing and the vapour-pressure working.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Memorise the five steps in order. Never skip Principle 1.
  • Intermediate: Set drying targets for every job. Place airmovers before you unpack chemistry.
  • Pro: Trade the CHAT dials against the drying load, and explain wicking and how to prevent it.

lessons.title: Spot or stain, and the six classes
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Explain the difference between a spot and a stain.
  • Name the stain class and first-line chemistry for a given soil.

A spot is something standard cleaning can remove. A stain has permanently altered the fibre's dye structure. Part of your professional judgement is knowing which one you are looking at before you spend two hours and the customer's patience on something that cannot come out.

ClassExamplesFirst-line chemistry
Water-solubleSugar, urine salts, most beveragesWater, or a mild alkaline spotter
Solvent-solubleOils, grease, lipstick, tar, gumSolvent, or a paint-oil-grease (POG) spotter
ProteinBlood, egg, dairy, vomitEnzyme or mild alkaline spotter in cool water
TanninCoffee, tea, red wine, tomatoAcidic spotter (wool-compatible when low in alkalinity), then an oxidiser if needed
DyeRed cordial, red wine pigment, inkHeat-assisted reducing agent or dye stripper
CombinationMost food spillsTreat each class in sequence

Insoluble soil such as clay, carbon or sand is a seventh group, and you remove it mechanically.

lessons.title: The decision tree and the three-attempt rule
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Work through the ten steps of the spot-removal decision tree.
  • Apply the three-attempt rule and disclose honestly.
  1. Identify the stain class.
  2. Test the planned chemistry in an inconspicuous area. Look for bleed, crock or distortion.
  3. Blot out as much as you can. Never rub.
  4. Apply cold-appropriate chemistry from the outside in. Wait out the dwell time.
  5. Blot out. Reapply once if there is partial improvement.
  6. Escalate: heat, then an oxidiser (for tannin and protein) or a reducing agent (for dye).
  7. Rinse-extract thoroughly. Over-applied spotter becomes re-soiling or wicking.
  8. Dry quickly and set an airmover.
  9. Reinspect at 24 hours. Some stains wick back from deeper in the fibre.
  10. If there is still no visible improvement after three attempts, stop. Then disclose it honestly.

Blot, do not rub

Rubbing distorts the pile geometry. The fibres separate from their natural alignment and the visible bruise stays even after the spot is gone. Blot-not-rub is not superstition. It preserves the pile.

Urine gets more alkaline with age

Fresh urine sits around pH 6. As bacteria break down the urea it turns to ammonia, and aged urine can climb to pH 10 to 12. That is why a fresh spot often responds to a general spotter, while an old yellow stain ignores alkaline chemistry and only gives way to an acid-side spotter. If you inherit a three-year-old pet problem and hit it with an alkaline pre-spray, you add alkalinity to a substrate that is already strongly alkaline. Acid-side first on aged urine, always.

The three-attempt rule

If a stain has not visibly improved after three rounds of the right chemistry, stop. You are probably looking at a permanent dye stain. Tell the customer plainly: "I can keep working, but I risk damage, and it is your choice." Damaged carpet costs more than a surviving stain.

lessons.title: The six-bottle spotting kit and chemical safety
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • List the six bottles in the minimum spotting kit and what each is for.
  • State the two chemical combinations you never make.
  • Acid-side spotter (wool-compatible, pH 2.5 or higher): tannin and urine that has set.
  • Alkaline-side spotter: general organic soil.
  • Protein or enzyme spotter: blood, dairy products and food.
  • POG solvent: adhesives, and gum softener.
  • Oxidiser (hydrogen peroxide, 3 to 12 per cent depending on the fibre): stubborn tannin.
  • Reducing agent (sulphite or bisulphite based): red cordial and other red dyes.

Chemistry compatibility

  • Never mix an acid spotter with chlorine bleach. It produces chlorine gas.
  • Never mix an oxidiser with a reducing agent. They cancel each other and can give off heat.
  • Rinse thoroughly between escalation steps.

Wear nitrile gloves and eye protection for every one of these.

Starting points from the product guide

The CARSI and CCW Product Guide gives these first picks as starting points only. Pre-test every one.

  • Fresh water-soluble spills: blot, then BioShot UHT at spotter strength (25 g per litre).
  • Tannin: e-Rinse EFR on the spot for 60 seconds first, blot, then flush with BioShot. Acid side first, never alkali first.
  • Protein: BioShot UHT in cool or tepid water with a 10 minute dwell. Hot water sets protein.
  • Oil, grease, gum or tar: CitraBoost neat on the spot for about 60 seconds, then flush with BioShot and rinse. Solvent first on oil. Freeze and chip chewing gum.
  • Rust, ink or red dye: use a dedicated remover from your supplier, not CitraBoost. Red-dye chemistry is fibre-specific. The guide says nylon only and never on wool.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Blot, do not rub. Identify the class before you pick the chemistry. Always test.
  • Intermediate: Run the five-step matrix and escalate cold first and heat second.
  • Pro: Know when to stop. Document the difference between a dye stain and a spot for the customer's records.

lessons.title: Why upholstery is not carpet
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Explain why a carpet method cannot be assumed to work on a sofa.
  • Name the four construction types and the risk each carries.

Upholstery is not carpet. Face fabrics are often more delicate, backings are unpredictable, glued trim and latex foam can run or collapse, and frame construction varies widely. The most common cause of upholstery damage is assuming that what works on carpet works on the sofa. It does not.

Construction types

  • Woven (plain, twill, satin, jacquard): the pattern depends on the weave, and loose weaves distort under agitation.
  • Tufted: yarn tufted into a primary fabric and commonly glued. There is a solvent risk.
  • Flocked: short fibres stuck to a base with adhesive. Often water-sensitive.
  • Non-durable constructions (chintz, quilted, moire, velvet): known to distort, crush or watermark under moisture.

Rayon lives here

Rayon turns up more often in upholstery than anywhere else: decorative throws, cushion covers and cheaper sofa fabrics. It can lose up to 70 per cent of its tensile strength when wet. On rayon, keep moisture low. Use dry compound, dry foam, or hot water extraction with tight dry strokes and fast drying.

lessons.title: Cleaning codes: W, S, WS or X
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Read a cleaning code and name a starting method for it.
  • Say why the code is a starting point and not a guarantee.
CodeMeaningStarting-point method
WWater-based cleaning is permittedWet methods: dry foam, encapsulation, hot water extraction rinse
SSolvent-based cleaning onlyDry solvent methods only, with no water
WSWater or solvent is permittedChoose by soil type. Wet is typical
XProfessional vacuuming onlyDo not attempt cleaning. Refer or decline

The code is a starting point, not a guarantee. Pre-test with the four tests in the next lesson whatever the tag says.

Starting points from the product guide

  • Code W: BioShot UHT at 25 g per litre, then e-Rinse EFR at 25 mL per 10 L as a fine-fabric rinse. For delicate weaves the guide suggests SnapShot Extra LMC at 8:1 as a low-moisture option.
  • Code S: dry-solvent method only, with no water-based product. Refer out if you have no dry-side training or equipment.
  • Code X: no chemistry. Dry vacuum and a soft brush only. Decline the job if the customer insists on cleaning. Honest refusal protects you.
  • Rayon, viscose or art-silk labelled items: low-moisture only.

lessons.title: The four-test pre-inspection
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Run the bleed and crock tests, then the shrink and distortion tests, and record each.
  • Explain why the shrink test is read at 24 hours.

Before you spray any chemistry on any upholstered piece, run four tests in an inconspicuous area and write each one down. If any test fails, stop. Rethink the method.

  1. Bleed: put a drop of water or pre-spray on a white cloth, press it flat and check the cloth for dye.
  2. Crock: rub a dry white cloth over the dry fabric and look for loose dye.
  3. Shrink: wet a patch about 50 by 50 mm, let it dry, and measure for any change in size.
  4. Distortion: apply the chemistry with gentle agitation and look for pile matting, weave separation or glossy spots.

Why 24 hours

Upholstery fabrics often shrink when wet and then spring back as they dry, partly or fully. Read the shrink test at 2 hours and a borderline fabric can look like a fail, so you turn away a job you could have cleaned. Read it at 24 hours and the fabric has either recovered, which is safe to clean, or it is still tight, which is genuinely unsafe. CARSI's protocol is to wet the 50 by 50 mm patch, dry it with low airflow, and measure at 24 hours and not before. The same protocol catches latex foam collapse, which shows up more slowly than weave distortion.

Common mistake: relying on the cleaning code alone and skipping the four tests because the tag says W.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Never clean without the four tests. Respect the X code.
  • Intermediate: Match method to fibre and construction. Flag non-durable fabrics before you quote.
  • Pro: Make the repair-or-restore call. Know when a piece is beyond scope and when an honest refusal is the service.

lessons.title: The six upholstery methods
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Name the six methods and what each is best for.
  • Say why you never use live steam on upholstery.

There are six recognised methods and each has its place. The live session compares all six on matched test sofas so you can see the speed, the residue and the finish side by side.

MethodBest forWatch-outs
1. Dry solventS-code fabrics and oily soilVentilation, and flammability on some products
2. Dry compoundDelicate or water-sensitive piecesResidue. Vacuum it out fully
3. Dry foamModerately soiled W-code fabricControl the foam moisture and rinse by extraction
4. EncapsulationLow-moisture maintenanceWorks well with a post-vacuum recovery
5. ShampooHeavily soiled, durable fabricResidue if not rinsed. Rarely a first choice today
6. Hot water extraction with a water rinseW and WS fabrics that can take itOver-wetting. Respect the fibre fence

No live steam

Hot water extraction on upholstery uses heated water, not live steam. Live steam above 100 degrees Celsius damages adhesives and glues, collapses latex foam and can distort delicate fibres. If a product advertises steam, check the real temperature at the tool.

Choose the least aggressive method that will clean the piece. Aggression rises as you go from dry compound to hot water extraction, and so does the over-wetting risk.

lessons.title: Olefin heat limits and tool tiers
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Explain why heat settings matter on olefin.
  • Compare the three tiers of upholstery tool.

Olefin and truck-mount heat

The manual gives olefin (polypropylene) a melt point of about 160 degrees Celsius and a softening point around 130 degrees. It states that a truck-mount can deliver solution at 105 to 120 degrees at the wand inlet on a cold boiler day, and more at the jet. A slow pass on olefin can flatten and gloss the pile for good. The CARSI rule is to dial the machine down to 60 degrees at the jet, keep the wand moving, and never make a second hot pass on known olefin. Check your own machine's output against its manual. That is why the method chart rates hot water extraction on olefin as high aggression.

Tool tiers

  • A 100 mm internal upholstery hand tool is the everyday staple.
  • A stainless hand wand gives more airflow and is rigid for cushion work.
  • An air-driven or external-jet tool is the fastest and over-wets the least, and it costs the most.

lessons.title: Speed-drying and the hands-on rotation
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Plan a speed-drying set-up before you apply chemistry.
  • Describe what you do and look for on the six-method rotation.

Speed-drying upholstery

  • Airflow first. Place one axial fan or small airmover to move air across the fabric, not into it.
  • Cut the humidity. Open a window or run a small dehumidifier if the room is above 60 per cent relative humidity.
  • Moving warm air beats still hot air. Air at 30 degrees on the move dries faster than still air at 60 degrees.
  • Target: hand-dry within 2 hours and fully dry within 6 hours on sturdy W-code fabric.

The rotation

On Day 2 you run all six methods on matched test pieces. Complete the four tests and the pre-inspection form first. Note the dwell time, the moisture you leave behind, the residue, and how long each piece takes to dry. The aim is for you to feel why a speed-drying plan and dwell discipline matter, not only to read about them.

Starting dilutions from the product guide for upholstery: BioShot UHT at 25 g per litre of warm water, and SnapShot Extra LMC at 8:1. Pre-test every time.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Six methods exist. Pick the least aggressive one that will clean the piece.
  • Intermediate: Plan a speed-drying set-up before chemistry. Know the trade-offs between tool tiers.
  • Pro: Make rescue-clean and salvage-clean judgement calls, and keep insurance-facing documentation.

lessons.title: Module 7 Knowledge Check: Upholstery Hands-On
Five hard-surface families
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Name the five hard-surface families and the weak point of each.
  • Run the vinegar drop test and read the result.

Hard floors are a natural add-on for a carpet cleaner because the customer already trusts you. The chemistry and the inspection rules are different, and the failures cost more. This module is inspection first, which is the habit that keeps you out of trouble.

FamilyExamplesWeak point
HardwoodSolid, engineered, oiled, sealedMoisture at the joints
LaminateHigh-density fibreboard core with an image layerJoints swell badly if saturated
StoneMarble, limestone, travertine, granite, slateCalcareous stones are etched by acid
Ceramic and porcelainGlazed and unglazed tileThe grout
ResilientVinyl, LVT, linoleum, rubberAlkaline for grease. Watch stripping chemistry

Calcareous and siliceous stone

Marble and limestone, along with travertine, are calcareous, which means calcium-based. Any acid etches them permanently. Granite and most slate are siliceous, which means silica-based, and they survive mild acid. Put a drop of distilled white vinegar on an inconspicuous spot. Fizzing means calcareous, and calcareous means never acid. Photograph the result with the date and location for the job file.

The mistake that costs the most is using an acidic grout cleaner on marble or travertine. The etch is instant and permanent, and it cannot be polished out without professional stone refinishing. A whole-floor resurface can run to five figures. That cost is CARSI professional judgement, not a quoted price. The vinegar test takes 30 seconds.

lessons.title: Non-destructive inspection
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Describe what a non-destructive hard-floor inspection allows and what it does not.
  • List the tools you carry and what the report must contain.

Under the scope of the hard-floor inspection standard, an inspection is non-destructive. You can measure and observe, and you can document and photograph. You do not pry boards, chip tiles or gouge sealer. The report has to be one you could defend.

Tools to carry

  • A moisture meter (pin and pinless types), set for the substrate.
  • A thermo-hygrometer to log room humidity and temperature at the time.
  • pH strips, distilled water and a white towel for surface chemistry.
  • A camera with a light, and a magnifier.
  • A tape, rule or calipers, a surface temperature reader and a straight edge or laser level.
  • Category-specific extras: a suction cup for laminate, expansion detection and feeler gauges for joints, a UV or IR light for moisture variation, and a gloss meter for ceramic.

Photographs

Date every photograph, put a scale reference in the frame, take several angles, and caption each one. If you did not photograph it, treat it as if it did not happen.

lessons.title: Cleaning starters by floor type
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Pick a safe starting chemistry for each hard-floor family.
  • Say where the product guide is honest about its limits for hard floors.
  • Sealed hardwood: neutral pH cleaner, damp mop only, never saturate the joints.
  • Laminate: damp microfibre, water kept off the seams. Laminate swells from the edge.
  • Marble and limestone: neutral-pH stone-safe cleaner only. No acid and no strong alkaline.
  • Ceramic: mild alkaline for grout soil, then a clear-water rinse.
  • Resilient (vinyl and LVT): mild alkaline for general soil. Use neutral maintenance products to protect the gloss. Avoid solvent boosters that can soften PVC.

The CARSI and CCW Product Guide says plainly that the supplier's published chemical range is carpet-and-upholstery focused as of April 2026. Stone-safe neutral cleaners, plus tile and grout chemistry and timber cleaners are best sourced by asking the supplier's counter, or from a specialist hard-floor supplier. For tile, the guide pairs the rotary extraction tools with a manufacturer-recommended tile and grout chemical. Never use e-Rinse EFR on calcareous stone.

Seal grout after cleaning it. Take a moisture meter reading before and after the job and log it, because laminate is moisture-intolerant and dry-side methods are preferred.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Never use acid on calcareous stone. Always test pH. Never saturate laminate joints.
  • Intermediate: Build an inspection report that would stand up to cross-examination.
  • Pro: Correlate moisture, relative humidity and time for cupping, buckling or tenting claims.

lessons.title: Module 8 Knowledge Check: Hard Floors
Why preventive maintenance pays
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Explain the difference between preventive and reactive maintenance.
  • Run the daily checklist, then the weekly and monthly ones.

Machines do not break down mysteriously. They wear in ways you can measure, and either you read the signs early or you pay a technician the hard way. The manual's rule of thumb is that every dollar spent on preventive maintenance saves about five to ten dollars of emergency repair and lost income. That is CARSI professional judgement, not a survey figure.

Daily (3 minutes before the first job)

  • Truck-mount oil level in the sight glass.
  • Belt visible, not glazed, and firm under a thumb press.
  • Jet spray pattern: pull the trigger into a bucket and check the fan.
  • Hose cuffs with no cracks, and fittings tight.
  • The RCD test button on the portable.

Weekly (15 minutes)

  • Vacuum test: measure the vacuum at the wand against your baseline.
  • Pressure test: measure the pressure at the wand against your baseline.
  • Listen for any new vibration or change in pitch from the blower or pump.
  • Clean all filters and lubricate the wand swivels.

Monthly (45 minutes)

  • Check the chemical pump rebuild kit if the hours are met.
  • Inspect the heat exchanger.
  • Listen to the blower bearings and grease them to schedule.
  • Check all electrical connections for corrosion.
  • Update the maintenance log with the hours, the date and the parts replaced.

The daily checklist catches most failures before they strand you on a job. The weekly pass covers vibration and sound, plus the suction benchmark. The monthly service adds years to the machine's life.

lessons.title: Truck-mounts, portables, rotary tools and wand sets
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • List the preventive checks for a truck-mount and a portable extractor.
  • Explain why you replace vacuum motor brushes before they fail.

Truck-mount

  • Blower oil: check the level weekly and change it at the manufacturer's hours interval.
  • Belt tension: inspect weekly and retension to specification.
  • Heat exchanger: flush yearly with a descaler and look for corrosion.
  • Vacuum relief valve: test it monthly.
  • Chemical pump: watch for a drop in output pressure and rebuild on schedule.
  • Winterise every autumn in frost-risk areas, with anti-freeze through the lines.

Portable extractor

  • Pump diaphragm: replace on a pressure drop or at the hours interval.
  • Filters: clean after every job and replace on schedule.
  • Vacuum motors: worn brushes shorten the motor's life, so replace the brushes before the motor.
  • Hoses and fittings: inspect for kinks, weeping leaks and cracked cuffs every use.

Rotary tools, wands, hoses

  • Rotary and counter-rotating brush tools: brushes typically last 80 to 120 hours, bearings are greased on schedule, and drive belts are checked for tension and wear.
  • Wand swivel joints: lubricate monthly and replace the seal kits yearly.
  • Jets: clear a blockage with a pin and check the spray fan.
  • Corner guards: replace them when worn so they do not snag the carpet.

Replace the brushes, save the motor

Carbon brushes on portable extractors and upright vacuums typically wear out at roughly 60 to 70 per cent of the motor's full life. Most technicians run them to failure. The worn brush then arcs on the commutator, pits the windings and usually writes off the motor. A pair of brushes is about $15 to $40 (Australian dollars, check current prices), and a replacement motor costs ten to fifteen times that. A good habit is to log motor hours, then pull and measure the brushes at 400 to 500 hours (new is about 25 mm, condemn at about 8 mm), and replace them in a ten-minute job.

Machine pressure is usually quoted in psi. 100 psi is about 690 kPa. Many vacuum gauges read inches of mercury, and 1 inHg is about 3.4 kPa. Record whichever unit your gauge uses, along with your baseline.

lessons.title: Six intervals and schedules for portable machines
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Use the six-interval system and the hours triggers together.
  • Match a portable machine to its care type and run the right schedule.

The schedules below come from the supplier's catalogue at ccwonline.com.au (checked July 2026) and the machine makers' published material. Your own machine's operator manual is the final authority. Where a manufacturer figure could not be confirmed, it is CARSI professional judgement.

The six intervals

Calendar intervals keep a low-volume operator honest. Hours-based triggers take over when you are busy, because a machine run eight hours a day hits its service hours long before the month ends. Whichever comes first wins.

IntervalPortable triggerTruck-mount trigger
DailyEvery job, and end of dayEvery job, and end of shift
WeeklyAbout 5 working days or 15 to 20 hoursAbout 5 working days or 20 to 30 hours
MonthlyAbout 20 days or 60 to 80 hoursAbout 50 to 100 engine hours
QuarterlyAbout 200 to 250 hoursAbout 300 engine hours
Half-yearAbout 400 to 500 hoursAbout 600 engine hours or mid-season
End of yearYearly or 1000 hoursYearly full service

Care type A: in-tank-heat portables

For example the Razorback SPOTX, TRACTX, Creed 220 and Balboa 220 and 500LW, sold through the roadshow partner.

  • Daily: check the spray fan at the wand, because a split or narrow fan is a blocked jet. Clean the vacuum inlet filter and shut-off float screen and make sure the float ball moves freely. At day's end rinse the solution tank, chemical line and pump with fresh water so no pre-spray or acid rinse sits in the pump overnight. Store with the recovery tank lid open.
  • Weekly: clean the solution filter, inspect the hoses and cuffs, and compare water-lift at the wand with your new-machine baseline.
  • Monthly: flush the chemical system with a manufacturer maintainer, clean the air inlet and check the dump valve seal.
  • Quarterly (about 250 hours): flush a white vinegar solution through the solution system to remove alkaline and hard-water scale. Use roughly 1 L of white vinegar to 8 L of water, then rinse with clean water. Check the in-tank heater element for scale and service the pump inlet filter.
  • Half-year (about 500 hours): pull and measure the vacuum motor brushes, and inspect the vacuum gaskets and lid seal.
  • End of year: have a qualified technician inspect it, replace the pump seal kit if the hours are met, and reconcile the machine log.

Care type B: dual heat system portables

These do everything in type A and also care for the inline heat exchanger that recovers heat from the waste vacuum air. After the fresh-water flush each day, run clean water through the exchanger. Descale the coil with the vinegar flush every quarter. At the half-year check, look at the exchanger fittings for scale weep and corrosion.

A scaled exchanger fails quietly. A dead in-tank heater gives you cold water and you notice at once. A scaled coil keeps working, but the solution arrives a few degrees cooler each month. Because CHAT lets you trade heat for dwell and chemistry, you make up for it without realising. The quarterly flush keeps the temperature you think you have equal to the temperature you actually have.

Care type C: auto fill and auto pump-out portables

For example the Drago 1600 Auto and Balboa 700 Auto. They do everything in types A and B and also need these: clean the debris screen on the pump-out each day, run the auto-dump with a full tank of clean water every fortnight to flush lint from the pump base, test the auto-fill float and shut-off monthly, and inspect the pump-out check valve and discharge hose quarterly.

lessons.title: Truck-mount schedule, hours card and machine log
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Follow the truck-mount schedule and identify your engine's oil interval.
  • Use the hours trigger card and keep a machine log.

Care type D: slide-in truck-mounts

A truck-mount is an engine, a blower, a heat exchanger and a high-pressure pump on one frame. Engine hours drive the schedule. Examples are the Sapphire 370EFI, Peak 500, Apex 570 and Everest 870HP, and the HydraMaster TITAN and Boxxer ranges and the TMTG4000.

  • Daily: flush the solution system and high-pressure pump with clean water, then empty the waste tank and rinse it. Clean the waste filter and the pump-out screen, check the engine oil on the sight glass or dipstick, check the coolant on liquid-cooled units, and look over the belts and hoses, and the fuel line, for leaks.
  • Weekly: compare vacuum and solution pressure at the wand with your baseline, check the blower belt for tension and glazing, listen for new vibration or pitch, and clean the water box and float filters.
  • Monthly: flush the heat exchanger, test the vacuum relief valve, grease to schedule and check electrical connections for corrosion.
  • Quarterly: change the engine oil to its interval, check the high-pressure pump rebuild kit if the hours are met, and descale the heat exchanger (yearly at a minimum, quarterly in hard water).
  • Half-year: change the blower oil and check the bearings, inspect the exhaust shielding and cooling belt, and inspect all vacuum and solution hoses.
  • End of year: full manufacturer service, reconcile the hours log, and winterise in any frost-risk region before the first cold snap.

The 300-hour trap

On a Kohler EFI engine with the extended oil life programme, such as the Sapphire 370EFI, the supplier's specification gives an oil and filter change every 300 hours with the approved synthetic oil and no 8-hour break-in change. Most other truck-mount engines need a first change at 8 hours and then every 50 to 100 hours. The expensive mistake is applying 300 hours to a non-EFI engine, which can cook the motor. The rule is not a number to memorise. Read the engine plate, then follow that engine's manual. Write the engine model on the front page of the log so a relief driver cannot get it wrong.

Example specification as published by the supplier in July 2026: the Sapphire 370EFI has a 26.5 horsepower Kohler V-twin EFI engine and a 341 litre aluminium waste tank. The Razorback Balboa 700 Auto portable has a single 10 amp cord and a pump motor rated 230 V at 3.6 A. Larger TRACTX units ship with 15 amp cords.

Hours trigger card

ComponentCheck or service atCondemn or act
Vacuum motor carbon brushesMeasure every 400 to 500 hoursReplace at about 8 mm (new about 25 mm)
In-tank heater or exchanger coilDescale about every 250 hours, or on hard waterVisible scale crust
Solution or high-pressure pumpPressure check weekly. Rebuild at the maker's hoursOutput below your baseline
Kohler EFI engine oilEvery 300 hours, approved syntheticNone
Non-EFI truck-mount oilFirst change at 8 hours, then every 50 to 100 hoursNone
Blower beltInspect weeklyGlazed, cracked or slack
Hoses and cuffsInspect weeklyCrack, weep or loose cuff

Machine log

Keep one page for each machine and reconcile it at the end of the year. Columns: date, engine or run hours, interval done (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, half-year, end of year), parts replaced, vacuum, pressure, notes, initials. On the front page, write the machine model, engine model and oil specification, pump model, your new-machine vacuum and pressure baselines, the cord rating (10 A or 15 A) and the service contact.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Run the daily checklist without skipping a day, and the weekly and monthly ones on schedule. Find your machine's care type.
  • Intermediate: Run the six-interval calendar and the hours card together, and log baselines each week. Descale on schedule, not on symptom.
  • Pro: Cost the downtime against the preventive spend, plan replacements 6 to 12 months out, and train relief drivers to the log.

lessons.title: Six cost lines and three pricing models
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • List the six cost lines and what each one captures.
  • Choose between per square metre, per room and minimum call-out pricing.

Technical skill without pricing discipline is charity. Customers do not pay for hours. They pay for the result and for trust. This module is the costing and communication framework CARSI-trained cleaners use to protect their margin.

Cost lineWhat it captures
1. Direct labourWages plus on-costs such as super and insurance, plus leave loading
2. ConsumablesChemistry, pads, pre-spray, tank water and detergents
3. Equipment amortisationThe truck-mount or portable replacement schedule
4. Vehicle and fuelCost per kilometre plus scheduled service
5. Fixed overheadRent, insurance, software, marketing
6. Profit marginWhat you take home after all of the above

Three pricing models

  • Per square metre: transparent and scales with the job. The default for commercial work.
  • Per room: simple for residential work and it anchors the customer's thinking to rooms.
  • Minimum call-out: covers low-value jobs and protects busy time slots.

Most profitable cleaners run all three at once and apply whichever model earns most for that type of customer. Know your break-even rate for each hour before you quote.

lessons.title: Callbacks and the moisture addendum
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Read your callback rate as a pricing signal.
  • Explain why a signed moisture addendum protects both sides.

Your callback rate is a pricing signal

These are CARSI benchmarks, from the trainer's professional judgement and not an industry survey. A well-run operation sees a customer-initiated rework request on about 3 to 4 per cent of completed residential jobs. It is never zero, because some wicking and slow-drying complaints come from physics, not poor work. Above 6 per cent, you are paying for rework out of your margin, and the fix is usually in the process: a second vacuum pass, a longer dwell and verified drying. Below 1 per cent often means you are over-delivering and under-charging, because the job is priced as standard but done as premium. Track callbacks by cause for a quarter (wicking, drying, residue, spot return). It tells you which CHAT dial your pricing is not paying for.

The moisture addendum

A short written disclosure signed at the start of the job protects both sides. Sample wording from the manual:

The customer acknowledges that carpet may remain damp to the touch for up to 12 hours after cleaning. During this time, walking on the carpet with shoes, placing furniture without protectors, or restricting airflow can extend drying time and in some cases lead to wicking of deeper stains back to the surface. The cleaner will set realistic drying expectations, place airmovers where agreed, and advise reinspection at 24 hours if any concern arises.

Have your own adviser read your wording before you use it. This is a sample, not legal advice.

lessons.title: Complaint scripts
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Use a calm script for a slow-drying, wicking or dye-bleed complaint.
  • Link each script to the record you kept at the time of the job.

Under pressure you do not invent wording. You recall it. In the workshop you role-play these in pairs, five minutes for each script, then swap roles.

Slow drying

Thanks for calling, [customer name]. I am glad you raised it early. A few things affect drying time: the humidity today, the airflow in the room, and whether the carpet is over a timber floor. Can you feel the carpet in a few spots and tell me if it is wet, damp or just cool? I will talk you through the next step.

A stain returns (wicking)

That is wicking. Deeper soil moves up as the carpet dries. It also tells us the stain was deeper than it looked. I will come back and treat the spot, and that is covered under our reinspection policy at no charge.

Only say that last line if it is your actual policy.

Dye bleed on upholstery

Thank you for showing me this. Dye bleed usually means the dye was not fully set at the factory. We test for it before cleaning, but some fabrics only fail during a full clean. Let me document what we are looking at, speak to my senior colleague, and call you back within [x] hours with a plan.

If you ran the four tests and recorded them, say so and show the record. That is what the pre-inspection form is for.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Know your break-even rate per hour. Use the six cost lines.
  • Intermediate: Quote a commercial contract using a frequency and throughput model.
  • Pro: Build an upsell pathway of protector and deodoriser, then inspection with a report.

lessons.title: How the council works
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Describe the three stages of the council review.
  • Explain why the personas are composite archetypes.

The CARSI Expert Council is a structured panel review. It applies seven composite expert viewpoints to a real-world cleaning or restoration case. It adapts the three-stage multi-perspective pattern published by Andrej Karpathy as llm-council, reworked here for people in a room. The framework is his, and CARSI credits it.

  1. First opinions: each council member gives an independent 60-second opinion on the case. No cross-talk.
  2. Anonymised peer review: the opinions are shared with the names removed. Each member ranks the other six from 1 to 6 and points out weaknesses.
  3. Chairperson synthesis: the Chair pulls the strongest points into one reasoned recommendation. Phill delivers the final teach.

Every persona is a labelled composite, a credentialled archetype and not a real person. No quote or opinion should be attributed to any living individual. The council is a teaching device that surfaces professional viewpoints, and the stage is designed to bring disagreement out before the group settles on a view. It is a reasoning pattern, not a checklist.

They want it back in use tonight and they have mentioned a cheap quote from a competitor. Run it through the council. The equipment engineer will ask what temperature your machine really delivers. The business coach will ask what the callback risk costs.

Then the Chair pulls it together: acid-side chemistry first on the aged urine, warm water and not hot, a low-alkalinity product, a signed moisture addendum, an honest talk about permanent dye change, and a price that covers the drying time.

A working cleaner rarely has seven experts on call. You can still run the method alone. Write the seven viewpoints on seven index cards, spend 60 seconds with each one on a tricky job, then pull it together. The exercise reliably shows up blind spots you could not see from a single point of view.

lessons.title: The escalation ladder and the chromophore
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Name the six rungs of the escalation ladder and what each one does.
  • Explain how oxidisers and reducing agents each switch off a chromophore.

Module 5 gave you the framework: identify the class, blot, go cold first, then escalate. Know when to stop. This module goes one layer deeper into the chemistry of escalation, the problem stains that beat beginners, and the spills you will actually meet in Australian homes and workplaces. It assumes you have the Module 5 decision tree, the six-bottle kit and the three-attempt rule.

Escalation does not mean trying a stronger product. Each rung uses a different chemical mechanism. Climb only as far as the stain forces you, and rinse between rungs, because a residue from rung 2 can neutralise rung 3.

RungMechanismUse forWatch-out
1. Aqueous spotterDissolve and suspendWater-soluble soilsOver-application leads to re-soiling
2. pH shift (acid or alkaline)Move the stain off its set pointTannin (acid) and general organic soil (alkaline)Match it to the fibre fence
3. Enzyme or protein digesterBreak protein bondsBlood, dairy, vomit, urine solidsNeeds dwell and warmth. Cool water first on blood
4. Solvent (POG)Dissolve non-polar soilOil, grease, gum, adhesive, inkVentilate. Some products are flammable
5. Oxidiser (hydrogen peroxide, 3 to 12 per cent)Break the chromophore by adding oxygenSet tannin, coffee, some dyesTest on the fibre. Can lighten some carpets
6. Reducing agent (sulphite or bisulphite)Break the chromophore by removing oxygenRed dye, cordial, some inksHeat-assisted. Never mix with the oxidiser

The chromophore

A stain is visible because part of a molecule, the chromophore, absorbs light. You do not have to remove the whole molecule. You only have to break the part that absorbs light. Oxidisers do it by adding oxygen and reducing agents do it by taking oxygen away. That is why a dye stain that ignores detergent can give way to a reducing agent. You are not lifting it. You are switching its colour off.

lessons.title: Problem stains: dyes, urine, tannin, protein, solvent soils
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Treat red dye, aged urine and tannin, then protein and oily soil, in the right order.
  • Say why heat is deliberate on red dye and forbidden on protein.

Cold first and test first apply to every entry below. All chemistry stays inside the fibre fence from Modules 2 and 3. On wool, keep acid-side products at pH 2.5 or higher and keep heat low.

Red dye: cordial, red sports drinks, some lollies

  1. Blot. Do not heat yet.
  2. Try an aqueous spotter first, because some fresh red is just water-soluble colour.
  3. If it holds, apply a reducing-agent red-dye remover, cover it with a damp white towel and apply gentle heat in short bursts. A steam iron over the towel works, or a low pass of the wand. Check every 30 to 60 seconds.
  4. Rinse-extract fully and reinspect at 24 hours. Never leave a reducing agent in the fibre.

Heat is the accelerator for the reducing agent, not the enemy. Red-dye reducers are the one deliberate exception to cold first, because they are designed to be heat-activated. The danger is heat on the wrong stain: it sets protein and tannin. So heat is the last rung, used only when you have confirmed a synthetic dye stain on a heat-tolerant fibre.

Aged pet urine: the three-year-old yellow

Fresh urine is about pH 6, and aged urine climbs to pH 10 to 12 as bacteria convert urea to ammonia. Alkaline pre-spray adds alkalinity to an already alkaline, dye-stripping substrate, so go acid-side first.

  • The real job is below the surface. The pad, the underlay and sometimes the floor hold the salts. Tell the customer that treating the surface is not decontamination.
  • Urine salts are hygroscopic. They pull moisture from humid air, and the smell returns on the next damp day. That is why the smell came back. It never left the underlay.
  • Escalate to an enzyme or oxidiser urine treatment with proper dwell for odour. Heavy contamination may need the floor sealed or the carpet and underlay replaced. That is outside a cleaning scope, so refer it or quote it as restoration.

Coffee, tea, red wine and tomato: tannin

Use an acidic spotter that is wool-compatible and low in alkalinity. If colour remains, use an oxidiser. Tannin is the textbook oxidiser stain. Rinse between rungs and never chase tannin with strong alkaline, which sets it and browns it.

Blood, egg, dairy or vomit: protein

Use cool water only, because heat cooks protein and sets it for good. Use an enzyme or mild alkaline digester with proper dwell. Vomit is protein plus acid plus food dye together, so treat it in sequence: protein first, then the dye.

Oil, grease, tar, lipstick, gum or adhesive: solvent-soluble

Use a POG solvent. For gum, freeze it and shatter it, or use a citrus gum-freeze solvent, then POG for the residue. Ventilate, because some solvents are flammable. Keep ignition sources away and use RCD-protected leads.

lessons.title: Problem stains: ink, rust, turmeric, nail polish, wax or colour loss
lessons.contentBody:
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • Choose the right chemistry for ink, rust, turmeric, nail polish and wax.
  • Recognise a bleach spot as colour loss and handle it honestly.

Ink

It depends on the ink. Ballpoint is oil-based, so use a solvent or POG. Water-based and gel inks respond to an aqueous spotter and then a reducer. Permanent marker needs solvent and you should expect only partial removal. Test a hidden area first, because some inks spread wider under solvent before they lift.

Rust: acid, never alkaline

Use a dedicated oxalic-acid rust remover. It is a strong acid, so ventilate, wear nitrile gloves, and keep it off calcareous surfaces nearby. Rinse thoroughly, because leftover acid re-soils and can damage the fibre dye.

Turmeric, curry or mustard

Common in Australian kitchens and share houses. The oil comes out first with POG. The yellow curcumin is a dye, so treat it with an oxidiser, and it is famously stubborn. Sunlight fades curcumin, so an honest "it will keep fading over a week in daylight" is often the truest advice. Say it may not clear fully.

Nail polish

Acetone lifts polish but it also dissolves acetate and some dyes and backings. Test hard. On a doubtful fibre, refer the job rather than risk a hole.

Candle wax

This is heat transfer, not chemistry. Scrape off the surface, lay a white blotter or paper towel on top and warm it with a low iron to wick the wax up into the paper. Then POG any dye residue. Do not start with solvent, because you will spread it.

Bleach spots are not stains

A bleach spot has removed colour, not added it, and no cleaner brings it back. It is colour repair, which means re-dyeing the affected tufts. Recognise it, disclose it honestly, and quote it as a repair or refer it. Never imply that cleaning will fix it.

The Australian spill profile

You will meet these more than anything else in Australian homes and workplaces: red cordial from kids' parties, coffee, red wine, turmeric or curry, pet urine, fake tan (a dihydroxyacetone stain that responds to an oxidiser), grass and clay on entry carpets, and sunscreen oil transferred to upholstery and vehicle interiors in summer. Stock the six-bottle kit plus a rust remover, a red-dye reducer and an oxidiser and you cover most of them.

Safety rules, repeated

  • Never mix an acid spotter with chlorine bleach. It produces chlorine gas.
  • Never mix an oxidiser with a reducing agent. They neutralise each other and can give off heat.
  • Rinse thoroughly between escalation rungs.
  • Wear nitrile gloves and eye protection for oxidisers, reducers, rust removers and solvents, every time.

Take-aways by experience level

  • Newby: Identify the class, test it, blot it, and start cold. A bleach spot is colour loss and not a stain. Never mix acid with chlorine or an oxidiser with a reducer.
  • Intermediate: Climb the ladder one rung at a time and rinse between rungs. Know which stains are oxidiser stains (tannin) and which are reducer stains (red dye), and why heat is deliberate on red dye and forbidden on protein.
  • Pro: Read sub-surface contamination and set honest expectations. Recognise colour repair as separate from cleaning, document a permanent dye stain for the customer's record, and stop at the three-attempt line.
